inline.s: With wisdom unobstructed as the Buddha himself, he walked the way of mercy’s care; as teacher of both gods and men he stood, the hero of the three realms beyond compare.
With the lion’s roar he preached the Dharma, ferrying every being,
(perfectly fulfilling the forty-eight great vows he had made in former days)
, and so all beings attained the Way
(causing every being born in my land to realize Buddhahood)

[Lion’s roar]When the Buddha preaches the Dharma, he is utterly without fear; his voice shakes the ten directions and subdues the host of demons, just as when a lion roars, all the hundred beasts are brought low.
[All beings attain Buddhahood]Causing all beings born in my land to realize Buddhahood. That is, as the forty-eight vows above declare:

“All sentient beings, as well as those in the Yama realm and within the three evil paths, who come to be born in my land and receive my Dharma-transformation, shall all attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.”
If these vows attain their fruit,
(if this vow is brought to pass)
, then the great-thousand worlds shall all be stirred,
(the great-thousand world system shall respond and tremble)
, and the gods in empty space shall rain auspicious flowers.]

[The Buddha told Ananda: when the Bhikṣu Dharmakāra had spoken this verse, at once the whole earth was shaken with six kinds of trembling. The heavens rained wonderful flowers, scattering them upon it. Of their own accord celestial music sounded, and from the sky a voice of praise declared: He is certain to attain supreme right awakening.]

The Buddha told Ananda: when the Bhikṣu Dharmakāra had spoken this verse, at once the whole earth manifested six kinds of trembling. From the heavens wonderful flowers rained down like rain, scattering upon it. In the sky music sounded of its own accord, and a voice of praise declared: He is certain to attain supreme right awakening (he is certain to become a Buddha).

[Six kinds of trembling]The six aspects of an auspicious trembling, namely: movement, welling up, shaking, striking, roaring, and bursting. These six kinds of trembling can be perceived and known only by one who has the heavenly eye; common people are wholly unaware of them. [A voice in the sky praising: he is certain to attain supreme right awakening]Because the Bhikṣu Dharmakāra had declared in the forty-eight vows: if any one of them were not fulfilled, he would never attain Buddhahood. “The voice in the sky praising: he is certain to attain supreme right awakening” is a prophecy that Dharmakāra will certainly become a Buddha, and that all the forty-eight vows will be completely fulfilled.

blocks.text: Amassing Merit and Virtue, Chapter Eight

inline.s: This chapter tells how the Bhikṣu Dharmakāra, through cultivation over immeasurable kalpas, amassed merit and virtue, thereby manifesting the Buddha-land
(“a dwelling vast and pure he gained”)
— the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[Ananda, after the Bhikṣu Dharmakāra had made these great vows before the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja and amid the host of gods and men, he dwelt in true wisdom, and with brave vigor and unremitting diligence single-mindedly set his heart on adorning the wondrous land. The Buddha-land he cultivated was vast and expansive, surpassing and uniquely wonderful, established to endure forever, without decay and without change.]

Ananda, after the Bhikṣu Dharmakāra had made these forty-eight great vows before the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja and amid the host of gods and men, he dwelt in true wisdom and cultivated with brave vigor and unremitting diligence, always single-mindedly bringing to adornment the wondrous land. The Buddha-land he was to cultivate was open and spacious, vast and grand, surpassing and uniquely wonderful, in every way the foremost. It would remain forever thus, never decaying or growing old.

[The Buddha-land he cultivated]The Buddha-land brought to cultivation is that which the Bhikṣu Dharmakāra, through his immeasurable, boundless realization of the wonder of merit, caused to manifest. The Vajra Peak Sūtra (Vajraśekhara) says:
“This Buddha-land alone is wholly formed by the pure vajra self-nature.”

[Established to endure forever, without decay and without change]The Buddha-land brought to cultivation (the Land of Ultimate Bliss), once established, remains forever thus, without such marks as decay or damage.

[Over immeasurable kalpas he accumulated and planted virtuous deeds. He gave rise to no thoughts of greed, hatred, delusion, or craving, and was not attached to the objects of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or thought. He delighted only in recollecting the wholesome roots cultivated by the Buddhas of the past. He practiced the practice of stillness and far removed himself from the false. Relying upon the gate of ultimate truth, he planted the roots of every virtue, never reckoning the many hardships.]

The Bhikṣu Dharmakāra, over immeasurable kalpas, accumulated and planted virtuous deeds. He gave rise to no thoughts of greed, hatred, delusion, or craving, and was not attached to the objects of the six dusts. He delighted only in recollecting the good cultivated by the Buddhas of the past. He practiced the practice of stillness and far removed himself from the false. Relying upon the gate of ultimate truth, he planted the roots of every virtue, never reckoning any hardship or distress.

[Six dusts]The dusts of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and thought. “Dust” means defilement, in that it defiles the human mind and prevents one’s true nature from being revealed. They are also called the six sense-objects, the external objects taken up by the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind). [Ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)]The true principle of the stillness of nirvāṇa seen by the sage’s wisdom is called the ultimate truth.

[With few desires and contentment, he sought solely the pure Dharma and benefited the multitudes of beings. His vows and resolve were never weary; the power of patience was accomplished. Toward all sentient beings he constantly cherished compassion and patience. With gentle countenance and loving words he exhorted and encouraged them. He reverenced the Three Jewels, served and attended his teachers and elders, and harbored no mind of pretense or flattery.]

He had few desires and was content, seeking solely the wholesome Dharma and benefiting the multitudes of beings. His vows and resolve were never weary; the power of patience was accomplished. Toward all sentient beings he constantly cherished compassion and patience. With gentle countenance and loving words he exhorted and encouraged them. He reverenced the Three Jewels, served and attended his teachers and elders, and harbored no mind of pretense or flattery.
[Pure Dharma]A general term for all wholesome dharmas. [Power of patience]The power of patient endurance. The Lotus Sūtra says:
“He also sees sons of the Buddha abiding in the power of patience; for those arrogant ones who revile and beat them, they are wholly able to endure, seeking thereby the Buddha-path.”
[Compassion and patience]Compassion and patient endurance. [Exhort]To advise and make clear. [Encourage]To urge so as to make one advance.

[He adorned all his conduct and was complete in the rules of practice. He contemplated all dharmas as like transformations, and his samādhi was ever still. He guarded well the karma of speech, never ridiculing the faults of others; he guarded well the karma of body, never losing the disciplines; he guarded well the karma of mind, pure and undefiled. To all cities and castles, villages and hamlets, kindred and jewels, he was wholly unattached. Endlessly he used the six perfections — giving, precepts, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom — to teach, transform, and settle beings, that they might dwell in the supreme, true Way.]

The Bhikṣu Dharmakāra adorned all his conduct and was complete in the rules of practice. He contemplated all dharmas as like transformations, and his samādhi was ever still. He guarded well the karma of speech, never ridiculing the faults of others; he guarded well the karma of body, never losing the disciplines; he guarded well the karma of mind, pure and undefiled. To all cities and castles, villages and hamlets, kindred and jewels, he was wholly without attachment. Always he used the wondrous practice of the six perfections — giving, precepts, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom — to teach, transform, and settle beings, causing them to dwell in the supreme, true Way.

[Rules and model]The standards that conduct should follow. [Contemplate all dharmas as like transformations]Contemplate that all dharmas are like illusions and magical transformations. [Discipline]The discipline is the precepts and the rules are the observances; these are what the practitioner should follow in establishing himself and in bearing himself in the world.

[Because he thus accomplished these roots of goodness, wherever he was born immeasurable treasures spontaneously appeared and responded. Now he was a householder or lay patron, of noble clan and honored rank; now a kṣatriya king or a wheel-turning sage-emperor; now lord of the six heavens of desire, even reaching the king of Brahmā. Before the Buddhas he honored and made offerings, never once ceasing. Such merits as these cannot be fully told.]

Because the Bhikṣu Dharmakāra accomplished such roots of goodness, wherever he was born immeasurable treasures spontaneously welled up. In his successive lives he was now a householder or lay patron, of noble clan and honored rank; now a kṣatriya king or a wheel-turning sage-king; now lord of the heavens of the realm of desire, even reaching the great Brahmā king of the realm of form. Before the Buddhas he honored and made offerings, never once ceasing. Such merits as these cannot be fully told.

[Immeasurable treasures spontaneously appear and respond]The Bhikṣu Dharmakāra, over many kalpas, accumulated the merit of giving and of moral precepts; therefore, in response, the treasures spontaneously welled up. [Householder (elder)]A general term for one who amasses wealth and possesses virtue. [Kṣatriya (shali)]That is, the kṣatriya, the second of the four castes of India. [Four castes]Brāhmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras. The Brāhmins were the religious of ancient India and held the highest authority; the kṣatriyas were the royal clan, honored equally with the Brāhmins; the vaiśyas were the general class of farmers, artisans, and merchants; the śūdras were the slaves who served others. [Six heavens of desire]The realm of desire (the world in which beings with the two desires of sex and food dwell) has six heavens, hence called the six heavens of desire: the heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the Yāma heaven, the Tuṣita heaven, the Nirmāṇarati heaven, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven. [Lords of the six heavens of desire]The kings of each heaven of the realm of desire. [Brahmā king]An abbreviation for the Great Brahmā king. [Realm of form]Above the realm of desire; because the beings of this realm have only a form-body and no desires of sex or food, it is called the realm of form.
[Now lord of the heavens of the realm of desire, even reaching the great Brahmā king of the realm of form]The Sūtra of the Mahāyāna Immeasurable Life’s Adornments (Song translation) says:
“Ananda, when the Dharma-practitioner Dharmakāra
(the Bhikṣu Dharmakāra)

, practiced the bodhisattva conduct, before the Buddhas he revered and honored them, attended and made offerings, never ceasing. As the Great King of the four heavens he constantly went to the Buddha’s abode, revered and worshipped, attended and made offerings. As the king of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven he constantly went to the Buddha’s abode, revered and worshipped, attended and made offerings. As the Yāma king, Tuṣita king, Nirmāṇarati king, and Paranirmitavaśavartin king, even as the Great Brahmā king and so on, he constantly went to the Buddha’s abode, revered and worshipped, attended and made offerings.”
[His body and mouth constantly emitted immeasurable wonderful fragrance, like candana
(zhān)

and utpala flowers, and that fragrance pervaded immeasurable worlds. Wherever he was born, his form and features were upright and adorned; the thirty-two marks and the eighty minor marks were all complete. From his hands constantly issued inexhaustible treasures and ornaments — all that is needful and most excellent — to benefit and gladden sentient beings. By these causes and conditions he could cause immeasurable beings all to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.]

By the power of his merit, the Bhikṣu Dharmakāra’s body and mouth constantly emitted of themselves immeasurable wonderful fragrance, like candana and the utpala flower, and that fragrance pervaded immeasurable worlds. Wherever he was born, his form and features were upright and adorned; the thirty-two marks and the eighty minor marks were all complete. From his hands constantly issued inexhaustible treasures and ornaments — all that is needful and most excellent — to benefit and gladden sentient beings. By these causes and conditions he could cause immeasurable beings all to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

[Eighty minor marks]Also called the eighty attendant marks, namely: the invisible crown of the head; the nose so high that the nostrils are not seen; the eyebrows like the new moon; the pendulous earlobes; the body firm and solid as Nārāyaṇa; the bones joined like a hooked lock; the body turning at a single motion like the king-elephant; the feet, when walking, four inches above the ground yet leaving the wheel-print; the nails red as copper, thin and glossy; the kneecaps firm, round, and fine; the body clean; the body soft; the body not crooked; the fingers round and slender; the finger-lines hidden and withdrawn; the veins deep and not visible; the ankles not visible; the body glossy; the body self-possessed and not stooping; the body complete; the countenance and deportment complete; the countenance and deportment fulfilled; the dwelling peaceful, with nothing able to move him; his majesty quelling all; all beings who see him delighted; the face not overlong; the countenance correct and the complexion unperturbed; face and eyes complete; the lips like the color of the bimba fruit; the voice deep and far-reaching; the navel deep, round, and fine; the body-hair curling to the right; hands and feet complete; hands and feet as desired; the lines of the hands clear and straight; the lines of the hands long; the lines of the hands unbroken; all beings, even of evil mind, made gentle at sight of him; the face broad and especially fine; the face pure and full as the moon; speaking gently and pleasantly according to beings’ intent; fragrance issuing from the pores; unsurpassed fragrance issuing from the mouth; the bearing like a lion; the advance and retreat like the king-elephant; the gait like the king-goose; the head like the madana fruit; all the parts of the voice complete; the four teeth white and sharp; the tongue red; the tongue thin; the hair ruddy; the hair soft and clean; the eyes broad and long; the marks of the death-gate complete; hands and feet red and white like the lotus; the navel not protruding; the belly not prominent; the belly slender; the body not swaying; the body firm and weighty; the body great; the body tall; hands and feet soft, clean, smooth, and glossy; the light about the body extending a full fathom; the light radiating about the body as he walks; looking equally upon beings; not slighting beings; not increasing nor diminishing the sound according to beings’ voices; preaching without attachment; preaching according to beings’ speech; giving voice in response to beings; preaching in due order by causes and conditions; all beings unable to exhaust the marks in gazing upon him; gazing without satiety; the hair long and fine; the hair not disheveled; the hair curling well; the hair blue-black as beads; hands and feet bearing the marks of virtue.

blocks.text: Perfect and Complete Fulfillment, Chapter Nine

inline.s: [The Buddha told Ananda: the Bhikṣu Dharmakāra, cultivating the bodhisattva conduct, accumulated merit and virtue, immeasurable and boundless. Over all dharmas he gained mastery, which cannot be known through words and discrimination. The vows he had made were perfectly fulfilled; he dwelt in truth, in a Buddha-land fully adorned and vast in majesty and virtue, pure and serene.]

The Buddha told Ananda: the Bhikṣu Dharmakāra, cultivating the bodhisattva conduct, accumulated merit and virtue, immeasurable and boundless. Over all dharmas he gained mastery, which cannot be known through words and discrimination. The forty-eight great vows he had made were perfectly fulfilled, and he dwelt in truth in a pure Buddha-land fully adorned and vast in majesty and virtue.

[Ananda, hearing what the Buddha said, addressed the World-honored One: The Bodhisattva Dharmakāra who has accomplished bodhi — is he a Buddha of the past? A Buddha of the future? Or a Buddha now present in another world?]

Ananda, hearing what the Buddha said, addressed the World-honored One: The Bodhisattva Dharmakāra, having become a Buddha — is he a Buddha of the past? A Buddha of the future? Or a Buddha now present dwelling in another world?

[The World-honored One declared: That Buddha Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes to nowhere; he is neither born nor extinguished, and is not of the past, present, or future. But in fulfillment of his vows, to ferry beings across, he is now present in the West, a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands distant, in a world named Ultimate Bliss. Dharmakāra became a Buddha, named Amitabha. Since becoming a Buddha, up to now, ten kalpas have passed. Now he is preaching the Dharma, surrounded and revered by immeasurable, countless hosts of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.]

The World-honored One told Ananda: That Buddha Tathāgata (Amitabha Buddha) comes from nowhere and goes to nowhere; he is neither born nor extinguished; he is not a Buddha of the past, of the present, or of the future. Only in fulfillment of his vows to ferry beings across widely, he is
now present in the West, a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands distant

, in a world named Ultimate Bliss. Dharmakāra became a Buddha, named Amitabha. Since becoming a Buddha, up to now ten kalpas have passed. Now he is preaching the Dharma, surrounded and revered by immeasurable, countless hosts of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.

[That Buddha Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes to nowhere; he is neither born nor extinguished, and is not of the past, present, or future]This is the ultimate truth, spoken with regard to the real mark of all dharmas.
[Now present in the West, a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands distant]The Sūtra of Immeasurable Life (Tang translation) says:

“The Buddha told Ananda: to the West, a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands distant, there is a world named Ultimate Bliss. The Bhikṣu Dharmākara attained Buddhahood there, named Immeasurable Life, and is now preaching the Dharma.”
The Amitabha Sūtra says:

“The Buddha told the Elder Śāriputra: from here, passing over a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands to the West, there is a world named Ultimate Bliss. In that land there is a Buddha named Amitabha, now preaching the Dharma.”
[Since becoming a Buddha, up to now ten kalpas]The Sūtra on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation) says:

“Ananda said to the Buddha: has the Bodhisattva Dharmakāra already become a Buddha and passed into cessation, or has he not yet become a Buddha, or is he now present? The Buddha told Ananda: the Bodhisattva Dharmakāra has now already become a Buddha, and is present in the West, a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands distant; his Buddha-world is named Peace and Bliss. Ananda again asked: since that Buddha accomplished the Way, how many kalpas have passed? The Buddha said: since he became a Buddha, in all ten kalpas have passed.”
The Amitabha Sūtra says:
“Since Amitabha Buddha became a Buddha, up to now ten kalpas.”

blocks.text: All Aspire to Become Buddhas, Chapter Ten

inline.s: [The Buddha told how Amitabha Buddha, as a bodhisattva, sought and obtained these vows. At that time Prince Ajāta and five hundred great elders, hearing this, were all filled with great joy. Each holding a golden flower-umbrella, they all came before the Buddha and made obeisance. Having offered the flower-umbrellas to the Buddha, they withdrew and sat to one side to hear the sūtra, and in their hearts made this vow: when we become Buddhas, may we all be like Amitabha Buddha.]

The World-honored One proclaimed how Amitabha Buddha, when a bodhisattva, after amassing merit and virtue, perfectly accomplished the forty-eight great vows. At that time Prince Ajāta and five hundred great elders, hearing this, were all filled with great joy. Each holding a golden flower-umbrella, they came together before the Buddha and made obeisance. Having offered the flower-umbrellas to the Buddha, they sat to one side to hear the sūtra, and in their hearts made this vow: when we become Buddhas, may we all be as excellent as Amitabha Buddha.

[The Buddha, knowing this at once, told the bhikṣus: these princes and the rest shall in the future become Buddhas. In their former lives they dwelt in the bodhisattva path and, over countless kalpas, made offerings to four hundred koṭis of Buddhas. In the time of Buddha Kāśyapa they were my disciples; now they make offerings to me and have met me again. At that time, the bhikṣus who heard the Buddha’s words all rejoiced on their behalf.]

The World-honored One, knowing at once the vow in their hearts, told the bhikṣus: Prince Ajāta and the five hundred great elders shall in the future become Buddhas. In their former lives they dwelt in the bodhisattva path and, over countless kalpas, made offerings to four hundred koṭis of Buddhas. In the time of Buddha Kāśyapa they were my disciples; today they come to make offerings to me and have met me again. At that time the bhikṣus who heard the Buddha’s words all rejoiced on their behalf.
